ts-prim-001.explanation: **The problem:** `string` vs `String` look interchangeable but aren't. **`string` (lowercase)** is the **primitive** type — the one you almost always want. **`String` (capitalized)** is the **wrapper object** type (instances of `new String()`), and it does **not** belong in annotations. **Why it matters:** the primitive `string` is *not* the same as the object `String`; a `String` object isn't assignable to a `string` parameter, and using the wrapper invites subtle bugs (e.g. `new String('a') === 'a'` is `false`). **The rule:** use lowercase `string`, `number`, `boolean` everywhere. **Common mistakes:** writing `: String`/`: Number`/`: Boolean` out of habit (some linters flag this), or constructing wrapper objects with `new String(...)`.

ts-prim-002.explanation: **The problem:** Remembering the three core type names. **The answer:** `string`, `number` (one type for ints *and* floats), and `boolean` — and conveniently, **each type name is exactly what JavaScript's `typeof` returns** for such a value (`typeof 'a' === 'string'`, `typeof 1 === 'number'`, `typeof true === 'boolean'`). **Why this is handy:** the mapping makes `typeof` narrowing intuitive — checking `typeof x === 'string'` narrows `x` to `string`. **Note:** TypeScript has one `number` type (no separate int/float), plus `bigint` for big integers. **Common mistakes:** using the capitalized wrapper types, or expecting separate integer/float types.

ts-prim-003.explanation: **The problem:** Do you have to annotate every variable? **No** — TypeScript performs **type inference**: it reads the initializer and assigns the type automatically. `let myName = 'Alice'` is inferred as `string` with no annotation. **Why rely on inference:** less noise, and the type stays correct as code changes. **When to annotate anyway:** function parameters (not inferable from a call), values initialized later, or to *widen/narrow* intent deliberately. **Subtlety:** `const` infers the **literal** type (`'Alice'`), while `let` infers the **widened** type (`string`), because a `let` can be reassigned. **Common mistakes:** over-annotating obvious initializers, or assuming inference reads your intent for empty arrays/objects (those may infer `any[]`/widened types — annotate those).

ts-prim-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** What does `any` actually do? **The answer:** it **turns off type checking** for that value — any property access, call, or assignment is permitted, and `any` is assignable to (and from) every type. It's an escape hatch that opts a value out of the type system entirely. **Why that's risky:** errors that types would catch slip through silently, and `any` is **contagious** — it spreads through expressions that touch it. **Why the other options are wrong:** it doesn't keep property checks (that's the difference from a typed object), it's the **opposite** of `unknown` (which forces narrowing before use), and it's not read-only. **The advice:** prefer `unknown` when you truly don't know the type (it's safe — you must narrow), and avoid `any` outside migration/interop. **Common mistakes:** using `any` to silence an error and masking a real bug.

ts-prim-004.explanation: **The problem:** When TypeScript can't infer a type, it silently falls back to `any` — quietly creating untyped holes (e.g. an un-annotated function parameter). **`noImplicitAny`:** a compiler flag that turns those **implicit `any`s into compile errors**, forcing you to annotate or let inference produce a real type. (It's part of `strict`.) **Why recommended:** implicit `any` is where bugs hide — it disables checking without you asking. Turning it on means every value is meaningfully typed. **Note:** *explicit* `any` (you wrote `: any`) is still allowed — the flag only catches the *implicit* ones. **Common mistakes:** disabling `strict`/`noImplicitAny` to 'make errors go away' (you lose safety), or leaving callback params untyped in flagged code.

ts-prim-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** What's the inferred type of `req.method` for `const req = { method: 'GET' }`? **The answer: `string`** — **not** the literal `'GET'`. **Why:** object properties are **mutable** by default, so TypeScript *widens* the property's type to `string` (you could later do `req.method = 'POST'`). The literal is only preserved when the value can't change. **How to keep the literal:** add `as const` (makes it `readonly` + literal `'GET'`), annotate the property, or pass the literal inline. **Why the others are wrong:** it's not the literal `'GET'`, not a union, and not `any`. **Common mistakes:** passing `req.method` to a function expecting a literal union and being surprised it's rejected (because it widened to `string`).

ts-prim-005.explanation: **The problem:** You want an object's properties kept as exact literal types (e.g. for a discriminated config), but they widen to `string`/`number` by default. **`as const`:** a const assertion that converts the value to its **most specific** form — every property becomes **`readonly`** and takes its **literal** type. So `{ method: 'GET' } as const` makes `req.method` the type `'GET'` (not `string`) and the whole object deeply readonly. **Why useful:** lock down config objects, tuples, and arrays so they're usable where literal types are required, and prevent accidental mutation. **Common mistakes:** expecting `as const` to do a runtime freeze (it's compile-time typing only — though it *forbids* writes at compile time), or applying it where you actually need a mutable value.

ts-prim-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** `let a = 'left'; printText('Hello', a)` errors when the parameter is `'left' | 'right' | 'center'`. **Why:** `let a = 'left'` is inferred as **`string`** (because a `let` is reassignable, the literal widens). `string` is broader than the literal union, so it's **not assignable** — TypeScript can't guarantee `a` is one of the three allowed values. **The fixes:** use `const a = 'left'` (infers the literal `'left'`), annotate `const a: 'left'`, write the literal inline, or assert `a as 'left'`. **Why the others are wrong:** literal unions *do* accept variables (if typed narrowly enough), `let` isn't categorically banned, and a cast isn't *required* in all cases. **Common mistakes:** storing a literal in a `let` and losing its narrow type.

ts-prim-006.explanation: **The problem:** `null` and `undefined` cause the most runtime crashes ('cannot read property of null'). **`strictNullChecks`:** when **off**, `null`/`undefined` are assignable to *every* type and used freely — TypeScript ignores them, so the compiler won't catch null-dereference bugs. When **on** (part of `strict`), `null` and `undefined` have their own types and you must **narrow** (check for them) before using a possibly-null value, or the compiler errors. **Why turn it on:** it surfaces an entire class of bugs at compile time. **How to narrow:** `if (x != null)`, optional chaining `x?.foo`, or a default `x ?? fallback`. **Common mistakes:** leaving it off (false sense of safety), or sprinkling `!` non-null assertions instead of genuinely handling the null case.

ts-prim-mcq-004.explanation: **The problem:** What does the postfix `!` (non-null assertion) do in `x!.toFixed()`? **The answer:** it **asserts at compile time** that `x` is not `null`/`undefined`, removing those from its type — with **no runtime check** generated. You're telling the compiler 'trust me, this isn't null here'. **The danger:** if you're wrong, it crashes at runtime exactly as untyped JS would — `!` only silences the type error, it doesn't protect you. **Why the others are wrong:** it doesn't throw, doesn't coerce to boolean (that's prefix `!`), and doesn't supply a default (that's `??`). **When to use it:** sparingly, when you *know* something the compiler can't prove (e.g. a value set just before). **Common mistakes:** scattering `!` to quiet errors instead of real narrowing, hiding genuine null bugs.

ts-prim-007.explanation: **The problem:** `bigint` and `symbol` are the lesser-known primitives. **Creating a `bigint`** (arbitrary-precision integers, ES2020+): the **`BigInt(100)`** function, or the **literal `100n`** (trailing `n`). Use it when values exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. **What's special about `symbol`:** every `Symbol('name')` call produces a **globally unique** value — so two symbols created with the **same description are never equal** (`Symbol('id') !== Symbol('id')`). That uniqueness makes symbols ideal as collision-proof object keys. **Common mistakes:** mixing `bigint` and `number` in arithmetic (a `TypeError` — they don't auto-coerce), or expecting symbols with equal descriptions to compare equal (use `Symbol.for()` for a shared registry if you need that).

ts-arr-001.explanation: **The problem:** Two syntaxes for array types look different but aren't. **The answer:** `string[]` (shorthand) and `Array<string>` (the generic form) mean **exactly the same thing** — an array whose elements are `string`. Pick one for consistency; `T[]` is the common house style. **Why two forms:** `Array<T>` is the underlying generic interface; `T[]` is sugar. The generic form can read better for complex element types (e.g. `Array<{ id: number }>` vs `{ id: number }[]`). **Common mistakes:** mixing both styles in one codebase (cosmetic, but lint rules often enforce one), or confusing `string[]` (array of strings) with a tuple `[string]` (a one-element tuple).

ts-arr-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Which line errors when `values` is `ReadonlyArray<string>`? **The answer: C — `values.push('hello!')`** — `push` (and other mutating methods like `pop`, `splice`, `sort`) **does not exist** on `ReadonlyArray`, because the type only exposes non-mutating operations. **Why the others are fine:** `slice()` (A) returns a *new* array without mutating, indexed *reads* (B) are allowed, and `length` (D) is a read. **Why it's useful:** declaring a parameter `ReadonlyArray<string>` (or `readonly string[]`) documents and enforces that your function won't mutate the caller's array. **Common mistakes:** trying to `push`/`sort` a readonly array, or assuming `readonly` blocks reads (it only blocks mutation).

ts-tuple-001.explanation: **The problem:** Sometimes you want an array with a **fixed length** and a **specific type at each position** (like a coordinate pair or a `[key, value]` entry). **A tuple type** does exactly that: `[string, number]` is an array that must have **exactly two** elements — a `string` at index 0 and a `number` at index 1. **How it differs from an array type:** `string[]` is any number of strings (all the same type); a tuple pins down both the **count** and the **per-index types**. **Why useful:** function returns of mixed pairs (like React's `useState`), `Object.entries` results, fixed records. **Common mistakes:** confusing `[string]` (a 1-tuple) with `string[]` (an array), or indexing a tuple out of bounds (TypeScript flags it).

ts-tuple-002.explanation: **The problem:** Tuples sometimes need flexibility — a trailing element that may be absent, or a variable number of trailing elements. **Optional element:** add `?` to a (trailing) element type — `[number, number, number?]` accepts 2 or 3 numbers. **Rest element:** spread an array type — `[string, number, ...boolean[]]` means a `string`, a `number`, then **any number** of `boolean`s. **Why useful:** model function arg lists, CSV rows, or `[label, ...values]` shapes precisely. **Rules:** optional elements must come after required ones; a rest element captures the remaining positions. **Common mistakes:** putting an optional/rest element before required ones (not allowed), or forgetting that an optional element makes the tuple's `length` a union (e.g. `2 | 3`).

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Rest elements in tuples

ts-tuple-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Assigning `pair[0] = 'hello!'` when `pair` is `readonly [string, number]`. **The result: a compile error** — index 0 of a **readonly tuple** cannot be assigned to; its positions are read-only. **Why:** the `readonly` modifier on a tuple type forbids writes to any element (just like `ReadonlyArray` forbids mutation), so the assignment is rejected at compile time (it never reaches runtime). **Why the others are wrong:** it's not a runtime TypeError (it won't compile), it doesn't mutate, and tuples *can* be indexed by literal numbers (reads are fine). **Why useful:** `readonly` tuples document that a function won't mutate a passed-in pair. **Common mistakes:** trying to mutate a readonly tuple, or thinking `readonly` only applies to objects/arrays and not tuples.

ts-obj-001.explanation: **The problem:** Not every object property is always present. **The `?` modifier** marks a property **optional** — objects of the type may include it or omit it entirely. **The catch under `strictNullChecks`:** when you *read* an optional property, its type includes **`undefined`** (it might not be there), so you must handle that before using it. **Why:** the compiler tracks 'this might be missing' and forces you to account for it. **How to handle:** a default (`opts.xPos ?? 0`), optional chaining, or a presence check. **Common mistakes:** using an optional property as if it's always set (error under strictNullChecks), or confusing optional (`xPos?: number`) with `xPos: number | undefined` (the latter requires the key to be present, possibly set to `undefined`).

ts-obj-002.explanation: **The problem:** `readonly` on a property — what exactly does it stop? **What it prevents:** **reassigning** the property — `obj.prop = 'x'` is a compile error. **What it does NOT prevent:** deep mutation. `readonly` is *shallow* — if the property holds an object or array, that value's **own contents can still be changed** (you just can't swap the whole reference). **Why:** `readonly` controls the binding, not the referenced value's internals. **For deep immutability:** use `readonly` recursively, `as const`, or `ReadonlyArray`/`Readonly<T>`. **Why useful:** signal 'this field is set once' and catch accidental reassignment. **Common mistakes:** assuming `readonly` deeply freezes (it doesn't — nested mutation compiles), or expecting a runtime guarantee (it's compile-time only).

ts-obj-003.explanation: **The problem:** Sometimes you don't know a type's property names ahead of time — only the *shape* of the keys and values (e.g. a dictionary). **An index signature** describes that: `[index: number]: string` means 'any `number` key maps to a `string` value'. The key type can be `string`, `number`, or `symbol`. **Why use one:** model dictionaries/maps, arrays-by-number, or config bags where keys are dynamic. **The constraint:** every *named* property must also be compatible with the index signature's value type. **Better alternatives often:** `Record<string, T>` (same idea, more readable) or a `Map` for true dynamic keys. **Common mistakes:** over-using index signatures where a precise interface or `Record` fits, or mixing incompatible named properties with the index value type.

ts-obj-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `createSquare({ colour: 'red', width: 100 })` fails even though `SquareConfig`'s properties are all optional. **Why: excess property checks.** When you pass an **object literal** directly to a typed slot, TypeScript checks for **unknown properties** and rejects them — `colour` isn't a known key of `SquareConfig` (it's a typo for `color`), so it errors *at the call site*. **Why this exists:** object literals are usually fresh and typos like `colour` are almost always bugs. **The escapes:** fix the typo, assign the literal to a **variable** first (excess checks only apply to literals), or add an index signature. **Why the others are wrong:** optional stays optional, all-optional interfaces *do* accept known properties, and the value types are fine. **Common mistakes:** misspelling a property and being confused by the 'optional' framing.

ts-obj-004.explanation: **The problem:** Two ways to combine object types — and they behave differently on conflicts. **`interface X extends A, B {}`:** inheritance-style composition; `X` gets all members of `A` and `B`. **`type X = A & B`:** an **intersection** type — a value must satisfy both. **The conflict difference:** if `A` and `B` declare the **same property with incompatible types**, `extends` is a **hard compile error at the interface declaration** (you must resolve it), whereas the **intersection silently types that property as `never`** (the impossible type — you only discover it when you try to use the property). **Which to use:** `interface extends` for object hierarchies you control; `&` for ad-hoc combination of types. **Common mistakes:** intersecting conflicting types and getting a confusing `never` later, instead of catching it at declaration.

ts-rec-001.explanation: **The problem:** You want an object type with a **known set of keys**, each mapping to the **same value type** (e.g. a lookup keyed by a union of names). **`Record<Keys, Type>`:** a built-in utility that constructs exactly that — keys of type `Keys`, values of type `Type`. With `Keys` as a literal union like `'miffy' | 'boris' | 'mordred'`, the resulting object must have **all** those keys (and no others), each holding a `Type`. **Why use it:** concise, enforced lookups/maps; missing a key is a compile error. **`Record<string, T>`:** allows *any* string key (like an index signature). **Common mistakes:** omitting a required key (error), or using `Record` when a precise interface with distinct value types is more appropriate.

ts-fn-001.explanation: **The problem:** How do you describe the *type* of a function (e.g. for a callback parameter)? **A function type expression:** `(a: string) => void` — list the parameters with types in parens, then `=>`, then the return type. `void` means it returns nothing meaningful. **Why useful:** type callbacks, higher-order function params, and variables that hold functions. **Note:** the parameter *names* in the type are just labels (they don't have to match the implementation); only positions and types matter. **`void` return subtlety:** a `() => void` type lets an implementation return a value — it's just ignored (handy so e.g. `arr.forEach(x => set.add(x))` works even though `add` returns the set). **Common mistakes:** confusing the function-type arrow with an arrow function, or thinking `void` forbids any return at all.

ts-fn-002.explanation: **The problem:** In JavaScript, functions are objects, so they can have **properties** (e.g. a `description`). How do you type a thing that's both callable *and* has fields? **A call signature inside an object type:** write the parameter list + return type **without** `=>` inside `{ }`, alongside the other properties — `{ description: string; (arg: number): boolean }`. That describes a value you can call *and* read `.description` from. **Contrast:** a plain function type expression (`(arg) => boolean`) can't also declare properties. **Why useful:** middleware/handlers with metadata, memoized functions with a `.cache`, etc. **Common mistakes:** using `=>` inside the object (that's a property whose value is a function, not a call signature for the object itself), or forgetting to attach the property at runtime.

ts-fn-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** What's the inferred type of `s` from `firstElement(['a','b','c'])` where `firstElement<Type>(arr: Type[]): Type | undefined`? **The answer: `string | undefined`.** **Why:** TypeScript **infers** the type argument `Type` from the call — the array is `string[]`, so `Type` = `string`, and the declared return type is `Type | undefined` = `string | undefined`. The `| undefined` is honest: an empty array would make `arr[0]` undefined. **Why the others are wrong:** it's not plain `string` (the function admits undefined), not `any`, not `unknown`. **Implication:** you must handle the `undefined` (optional chaining or a check) before using `s` as a string. **Common mistakes:** assuming generic inference drops the `| undefined`, or indexing arrays without accounting for possibly-missing elements.

ts-fn-003.explanation: **The problem:** A generic function sometimes needs to *use* a capability of its type parameter (e.g. read `.length`), but a bare `<Type>` could be anything. **A constraint** — `<Type extends { length: number }>` — **limits** which types are allowed for `Type`: only ones that have a numeric `length`. In exchange, the function body may safely access `.length`. **Why:** it keeps the function generic (works for strings, arrays, anything with `length`) while guaranteeing the members it relies on. **The trade-off:** you can only use what the constraint guarantees, not arbitrary members. **Common mistakes:** accessing a property inside a generic without constraining it (error — the parameter might not have it), or over-constraining so the function becomes less reusable.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Working with constrained values

ts-fn-004.explanation: **The problem:** Generics are easy to over-engineer. **The Handbook's three guidelines:** (1) **Push type parameters down** — prefer `<T>(arr: T[])` over `<T extends any[]>(arr: T)`; relate the parameter to the *element* type so inference and return types stay precise. (2) **Use as few type parameters as possible** — every extra one is more for callers to reason about. (3) **A type parameter should appear at least twice** — its job is to *relate* things (e.g. an input to the output); if it's used only once, it isn't relating anything and probably shouldn't be generic at all. **Why:** simpler signatures infer better and are easier to use. **Common mistakes:** adding type parameters that appear once (a sign a plain type would do), or constraining the whole array instead of the element.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Guidelines for Writing Good Generic Functions

ts-fn-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** With overloads `makeDate(timestamp)` and `makeDate(m, d, y)`, calling `makeDate(5, 5)` fails. **Why:** when a function has **overload signatures**, only those **overloads** are callable — the **implementation signature is not visible** to callers. Neither overload accepts exactly **two** arguments (one takes 1, the other 3), so the 2-arg call matches nothing. The implementation's `(mOrTimestamp, d?, y?)` is just there to *implement* both overloads, not to be called. **The fix:** add an overload for 2 args if it's valid, or call with 1 or 3. **Why the others are wrong:** optional params *are* allowed in the implementation; explicit type args aren't required; the overloads don't 'conflict'. **Common mistakes:** writing an implementation signature looser than the overloads and expecting callers to use it.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Overload signatures and the implementation

ts-fn-005.explanation: **The problem:** Three special return types confuse people. **`void`:** the return value should be **ignored** — the function may technically return something, but callers shouldn't rely on it (common for callbacks/side-effects). **`unknown`:** the function **does** return a value, but it could be anything, so you **must narrow** it before use — it's the type-safe alternative to `any`. **`never`:** the function **never returns at all** — it always throws or loops forever (exhaustiveness checks and error helpers use it). **Why distinguish:** they encode very different intentions about the result. **Common mistakes:** using `any` instead of `unknown` for 'I don't know the type' (loses safety), confusing `void` (ignore the result) with `never` (no result ever), or annotating a throwing helper as `void` instead of `never`.

ts-fn-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** Does `const f1: voidFunc = () => true` compile, where `type voidFunc = () => void`? **The answer: yes.** A **contextual `void` return type allows the implementation to return a value** — the value is simply **ignored**. This deliberate rule exists so you can pass functions that happen to return something to APIs that expect `() => void` (e.g. `array.forEach(x => mySet.add(x))`, where `add` returns the set). **The nuance:** the *call result* through the `void` type is still typed `void` — you can't use the returned value via that type. **Why the others are wrong:** returning a value is allowed (not forbidden), nothing is coerced to `undefined` at runtime (the value is returned, just type-erased), and arrow functions assign fine. **Common mistakes:** assuming `() => void` bans all returns.

ts-fn-006.explanation: **The problem:** How do you make a parameter optional? **Two ways:** (1) the **`?` modifier** — `function f(x?: number)` — makes `x` of type `number | undefined`; callers may omit it (and you handle the undefined). (2) a **default value** — `function f(x = 10)` — if omitted (or `undefined`), `x` becomes `10`, and its type is inferred from the default (`number`), so the body sees a guaranteed value. **Which to use:** `?` when 'absent' is meaningful and you'll branch on it; a default when you have a sensible fallback. **Note:** optional/defaulted params must come **after** required ones. **Common mistakes:** combining `?` and a default redundantly, putting an optional param before a required one, or forgetting that with `?` the value can be `undefined` inside the body.

ts-fn-007.explanation: **The problem:** `Math.atan2(...args)` fails for `const args = [8, 5]`. **Why:** `args` is inferred as **`number[]`** — an array of *unknown length*. But `atan2` needs **exactly two** arguments, and a spread of a variable-length array could supply any number, so TypeScript rejects it ('a spread argument must have a tuple type or be passed to a rest parameter'). **The fix:** make the length fixed with **`as const`** — `const args = [8, 5] as const` gives the type `readonly [8, 5]` (a 2-tuple), which matches the two-argument signature. **Why it matters:** tuples carry length information that arrays don't. **Common mistakes:** spreading a plain array into a fixed-arity function, or forgetting `as const` (or an explicit tuple type) to pin the length.

ts-fn-008.explanation: **The problem:** A callback's body uses `this`, and you want it typed (e.g. a predicate that runs with a `User` as `this`). **The solution:** declare a **`this` pseudo-parameter** as the **first** parameter of the function type — `(this: User) => boolean`. It types `this` *only*; it's **erased** at compile time, so callers don't (and can't) pass it as a real argument. **Why:** lets you safely access `this.admin` etc. inside the callback while keeping the call signature normal. **Important:** a function using a typed `this` must be a **regular function** (not an arrow — arrows have lexical `this` and can't declare the pseudo-parameter). **Common mistakes:** using an arrow function where a `this`-typed callback is required, or thinking `this` is an actual argument callers supply.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Declaring this in a Function

ts-iface-001.explanation: **The problem:** Two ways to name an object shape — which to use? **A type alias:** `type Point = { x: number; y: number }`. **An interface:** `interface Point { x: number; y: number }`. **For plain object shapes they're used identically** — both name a structure you can reuse and implement. **The differences show up elsewhere:** interfaces support **declaration merging** and read naturally for object/class contracts; type aliases can also name **unions, tuples, primitives, and mapped/conditional types** that interfaces can't. **Rule of thumb (TS docs):** prefer `interface` for object/class shapes until you need a feature only `type` provides. **Common mistakes:** thinking one is strictly 'better', or trying to write a union with an interface (use a `type`).

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Type Aliases vs Interfaces

ts-iface-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** What can an `interface` do that a `type` alias can't? **The answer: declaration merging** — declaring an interface **twice with the same name** combines (merges) the declarations into one type with all members. Type aliases can't be reopened like this — a duplicate `type` name is an error. **Why it exists:** it lets you *augment* existing interfaces (e.g. add properties to `Window` or a library's types). **Why the others are wrong:** type aliases *can* describe unions (`number | string`), can be 'extended' via intersections, and can be used as parameter types — those aren't interface-exclusive. **Caution:** merging is powerful but can surprise readers; prefer it for intentional augmentation. **Common mistakes:** accidentally declaring two same-named interfaces and getting unexpected merged members.

ts-iface-002.explanation: **The problem:** Adding members to an existing type with each form. **Interface:** use `extends` — `interface Bear extends Animal { honey: boolean }`. You can extend multiple interfaces. **Type alias:** use an **intersection** — `type Bear = Animal & { honey: boolean }`. **Both produce the same shape** (everything in `Animal` plus `honey`). **The subtle difference:** on conflicting members, `extends` raises a clear error at the declaration, while an intersection silently makes the conflicting property `never` (see object combination rules). **Which to use:** `extends` for object/class hierarchies; `&` when composing type aliases or unions. **Common mistakes:** mixing the two styles inconsistently, or expecting `&` to error on conflicts the way `extends` does.

ts-union-001.explanation: **The problem:** A value typed `number | string` could be either — what can you do with it? **A union type** is formed from two or more types; the value is **exactly one** of them, but the compiler doesn't know which. **So before narrowing, you can only use operations valid for *every* member** of the union (the common subset) — e.g. `.toString()` works for both `number` and `string`, but `.toUpperCase()` (string-only) is rejected. **To use member-specific operations, narrow first** (`typeof`, checks, etc.) so the compiler knows the concrete type in that branch. **Why:** safety — calling a string method on a number would crash. **Common mistakes:** trying to call a method that only exists on one member without narrowing, or reaching for `as` instead of a real `typeof` check.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Working with union types

ts-assert-001.explanation: **The problem:** Sometimes *you* know a value's specific type but TypeScript can't infer it (e.g. `document.getElementById` returns the general `HTMLElement | null`). **A type assertion** (`value as T`, or `<T>value`) tells the compiler to **treat the value as a more specific type** you're claiming it has. **The crucial caveat:** assertions are a **compile-time only** instruction — at runtime they're **completely erased**, performing **no check and no conversion**. If you assert wrongly, nothing stops the bad value; you just lose the compiler's protection. **Allowed scope:** you can assert to a more/less specific type with overlap; nonsense conversions need `as unknown as T`. **Common mistakes:** treating `as` like a runtime cast/parse (it isn't), or asserting to silence errors and masking real type mismatches.
ts-assert-001.example:
```ts
const value: unknown = 'hello world';

const str = value as string;  // 'trust me, it's a string'
console.log(str.length);       // works — it really is a string at runtime

const n = value as number;     // compiler allows it (from unknown) — NO runtime check
console.log(typeof n);         // 'string' — the assertion converted nothing
```

ts-gen-001.explanation: **The problem:** An identity function should return whatever type it received. Typing it with `any` 'works' but **throws away the type** — pass a string, get back `any`, and all checking stops downstream. **The generic version** `identity<Type>(arg: Type): Type` **captures** the argument's type in `Type` and returns the same type, so `identity('myString')` is typed **`string`** and `identity(42)` is `number`. **Why generics win:** they *relate* the input type to the output type, preserving safety and editor help, instead of erasing it like `any`. **The mental model:** a generic is a placeholder the compiler fills in per call. **Common mistakes:** reaching for `any` for 'flexible' functions (loses everything), or adding a type parameter that doesn't relate input to output (then it's pointless).

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Hello World of Generics

ts-gen-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `loggingIdentity<Type>(arg: Type)` fails on `arg.length`. **Why:** `Type` is **unconstrained** — it could be *any* type, and **not all types have a `.length`** (a `number` doesn't). So the compiler can't guarantee the property exists and rejects the access. **The fix:** constrain the parameter to types that *do* have it — `<Type extends { length: number }>` — or accept `Type[]` if you meant an array. **Why the others are wrong:** generic params *can* have constrained properties accessed, `length` isn't reserved, and the issue isn't a missing explicit type argument. **The principle:** inside a generic you may only use what the type parameter's constraint guarantees. **Common mistakes:** assuming a type parameter has members it might not, instead of constraining it.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Working with generic type variables

ts-gen-002.explanation: **The problem:** How do interfaces and classes take type parameters? **Put the type parameter list after the name.** **Generic interface:** `interface GenericIdentityFn<Type> { (arg: Type): Type }` — the whole interface is parameterized, so you pick `Type` when you use it (`GenericIdentityFn<number>`). **Generic class:** `class Box<T> { … }` — `T` is available across the class's members (fields, methods, constructor). **Why:** lets one definition work for many types while staying type-safe (a `Box<string>`'s `contents` is `string`). **Note (strict mode):** class fields must be initialized — do it in the constructor (or use `!`). **Common mistakes:** forgetting to supply/let infer the type argument, putting the parameter in the wrong place, or leaving generic class fields uninitialized under `strictPropertyInitialization`.

ts-gen-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** What does `Key extends keyof Type` do in `getProperty<Type, Key extends keyof Type>(obj: Type, key: Key)`? **The answer:** it **restricts `key` to the actual property names of `obj`**. `keyof Type` is the union of `Type`'s keys; constraining `Key` to it means you can only pass a real key — so for `{ a, b, c }`, `getProperty(x, 'a')` is fine but `getProperty(x, 'm')` is a **compile error**. Bonus: the return type is precisely `Type[Key]` (the value type for that key). **Why the others are wrong:** it doesn't convert keys at runtime, doesn't return `any`, and doesn't require all-string values. **Why useful:** type-safe property access/lookup helpers. **Common mistakes:** using a plain `string` key (loses the safety and precise return type), or forgetting the constraint and allowing invalid keys.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Using Type Parameters in Generic Constraints

ts-gen-003.explanation: **The problem:** A factory function receives a **class** and should return an **instance** of it, correctly typed. **The solution — a construct signature:** type the class parameter with `{ new (): Type }` (or the shorthand `new () => Type`), which says 'something you can call with `new` to get a `Type`'. The function returns `new c()`, typed as `Type`. **Why a construct signature:** a class used as a *value* is its constructor function; describing it with `new (): Type` lets TypeScript infer the instance type. **Why useful:** generic factories, dependency injection, plugin systems. **Common mistakes:** typing the parameter as the instance type instead of the constructor (you'd pass `new Dog()` rather than `Dog`), or forgetting the constructor's parameters if it requires arguments (`new (arg: X) => Type`).

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Using Class Types in Generics

ts-class-001.explanation: **The problem:** A class field declared but never set is a null/undefined bug waiting to happen. **`strictPropertyInitialization`** (part of `strict`) requires every declared field to be **initialized** — either inline (`name = 'x'`) or **in the constructor** — otherwise it's a compile error. **The `!` (definite assignment assertion):** placed after a field name (`name!: string`), it **opts that field out** of the check, telling the compiler 'this will be assigned before use, trust me' — useful when a framework, lifecycle method, or DI sets it later. **The risk:** like `!` elsewhere, it's an unchecked promise — if you're wrong, you get `undefined` at runtime. **Common mistakes:** declaring fields without initializing them (error under strict), or sprinkling `!` to silence the check instead of initializing properly.

ts-class-002.explanation: **The problem:** A field should be set once at construction and never changed afterward. **`readonly` on a class field** allows assignment **inline** (at the declaration) and **inside the constructor**, but **forbids assignment anywhere else** — any later `this.field = …` in a method is a compile error. **Why:** it documents and enforces immutability of the binding after construction. **The same shallow caveat as object `readonly`:** if the field holds an object, that object's contents can still be mutated — only reassigning the field is blocked. **Why useful:** ids, configuration, injected dependencies. **Common mistakes:** trying to reassign a `readonly` field in a method, or assuming it deep-freezes the referenced value.

ts-class-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `class NameChecker implements Checkable { check(s) {…} }` — what's the type of `s`? **The answer: `any`** — an `implements` clause only **checks** that the class is *compatible* with the interface; it does **not** add type information to the members. So `s` gets no contextual type from the interface and is **implicitly `any`** (and under `noImplicitAny`/`strict`, that's actually a compile error you must fix by annotating). **Why the others are wrong:** the type isn't inherited from the interface signature, unannotated params don't default to `unknown` or `never`. **The fix:** annotate the parameter yourself — `check(s: string)`. **The principle:** `implements` is a compatibility check, not a source of types. **Common mistakes:** expecting method/param types to flow from the implemented interface.

ts-class-003.explanation: **The problem:** Controlling who can access a class member. **The three modifiers:** **`public`** (the default) — accessible **everywhere**. **`protected`** — accessible **inside the class and its subclasses**, not from outside instances. **`private`** — accessible **only within the declaring class itself** (not even subclasses). **Why:** encapsulation — expose a clean API while hiding internals, and let subclasses build on protected members. **Important caveat:** these are **compile-time** checks (TypeScript only) — they don't truly hide data at runtime (use JavaScript's `#private` fields for hard runtime privacy). **Common mistakes:** assuming `private` protects data at runtime, expecting subclasses to reach `private` members (they can't — use `protected`), or over-annotating `public` (it's the default).

ts-class-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** `new MySafe()['secretKey']` where `secretKey` is `private` — what prints? **The answer: `12345`** — and notably it even **type-checks**. **Why:** TypeScript's `private` is a **compile-time-only** visibility check; at runtime the field is an ordinary property that exists on the object. Worse, **bracket access with a string literal** (`s['secretKey']`) is a known escape hatch that bypasses the privacy check at compile time too. **Why the others are wrong:** the field isn't stripped from the emitted object, it doesn't throw, and bracket notation compiles. **The lesson:** for *real* runtime privacy, use JavaScript's `#private` fields (`#secretKey`), which are truly inaccessible from outside. **Common mistakes:** trusting TS `private` to hide secrets at runtime.

ts-class-004.explanation: **The problem:** The boilerplate of declaring a field, adding a constructor parameter, and assigning `this.x = x` for each dependency. **Parameter properties** collapse all three: prefix a **constructor parameter** with a visibility modifier (`public`/`protected`/`private`) or `readonly`, and TypeScript automatically **declares a field of the same name and assigns the argument to it**. So `constructor(public readonly x: number)` creates a public readonly `x` field set from the argument — no extra code. **Why useful:** concise dependency injection and value objects. **Note:** you must include a modifier for it to become a field — a plain parameter stays just a parameter. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the modifier (then it's not a field), or mixing parameter properties with manual `this.x =` assignments redundantly.

ts-class-005.explanation: **The problem:** You want a base class that defines shared behavior but **shouldn't be instantiated on its own**, and forces subclasses to fill in specifics. **An abstract class** (`abstract class Base`) can't be instantiated with `new` — it exists only to be **extended**. **An `abstract` member** has **no implementation**; every **concrete subclass must implement it**, or the subclass is itself abstract. Non-abstract methods can call abstract ones (the template-method pattern). **Why:** enforce a contract while sharing common code. **Difference from an interface:** an abstract class can contain real implementations and state, not just signatures. **Common mistakes:** trying to `new` an abstract class (error), forgetting to implement an abstract member in a subclass, or using an abstract class where a simple interface would do.

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Abstract Classes and Members

ts-class-006.explanation: **The problem:** `static defaultValue: Type` inside `class Box<Type>` is an error — why? **Static members** belong to the **class itself**, not to instances — you access them as `Box.x`, not `new Box().x`, and there's exactly **one** static slot shared across every instantiation. **Why they can't reference the type parameter:** `Type` is **erased at runtime** and is chosen *per instance* (`Box<string>` vs `Box<number>`), but the static lives once on the shared class object — there's no single `Type` for it to be. So a static member's type can't depend on the class's type parameter. **The fix:** make the static non-generic, or make the member an instance member. **Common mistakes:** trying to store a generic default as a static, or expecting `Box<string>.x` and `Box<number>.x` to be different (they're the same slot).

resources.label: TypeScript Handbook — Static and type parameters

ts-class-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** A class has `get size()` but no matching `set size()`. **The effect: the property becomes automatically `readonly`** — reading `obj.size` works, but **assigning** to it is a **compile error**. **Why:** with only a getter, there's no defined way to write the value, so TypeScript treats it as read-only (this changed in TS 4.3+; older versions inferred a permissive setter). **Why the others are wrong:** assignments aren't silently ignored (they error), a getter doesn't require a setter, and it doesn't return undefined. **The fix if you need writes:** add a `set size(v) {…}` accessor. **Why useful:** computed/derived read-only properties (e.g. `area`, `fullName`). **Common mistakes:** trying to assign to a getter-only property, or adding a no-op setter when read-only is what you actually want.

ts-class-007.explanation: **The problem:** Subtle bugs come from misunderstanding *when* fields and constructors run in a class hierarchy. **The order when you `new` a derived class:** **base fields → base constructor → derived fields → derived constructor**. The base must be fully initialized before the derived part builds on it. **The rule that follows:** a derived constructor **must call `super()` before referencing `this`** — because `this`'s base portion isn't initialized until `super()` runs, touching `this` first is a compile error (and would be unsafe). **Why it matters:** derived field initializers run *after* `super()`, so a base constructor that calls an overridden method may see derived fields still undefined. **Common mistakes:** using `this` before `super()`, or relying on derived fields inside a base constructor (they're not set yet).
